This is an odd structure so worth spelling out.
-Staked tokens may receive up to 20% of equity for conversion if they were staked for 4+ years
-after a liquidity event (ie, IPO), the token will presumably lose a huge % of value and be reduced to a utility token. Unstaked tokens or tokens staked for less than 1 year miss out on the equity conversion (if IPO ever happens)
-the equity entity holds 37.5% of the token in reserve but it’s locked until 1 year after. I am unsure if there is any information about what would be done with the tokens 1 year after IPO— but to the extent that it retains value, one could assume the team/investors may further benefit from these tokens
-the other 37.5% is released on certain milestones (ie, licensing on certain markets, growth, etc)

Despite “public information” there are many misleading aspects.
-Many investors shilling this as “their highest conviction investment”. The audience reading can only buy the token when they actually bought equity. At least some of that at $100m FDV. As laid out above, the token is entitled to a maximum of 20% of the equity and only under certain conditions (IPO + long term staking), so this is not an apples to apples comparison. Some more transparency would be a bare minimum ask. It’s fair to assume by the time of IPO, 62.5% of tokens will be circulating. At the current price of $1.25, token buyers are paying $4B valuation pre-any IPO or pre IPO dilution for an option to convert into Backpack equity. The investors encouraging people to buy tokens bought something 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 and vastly superior 
-writing long-form puff pieces that provide no revenue numbers or trajectory. In the light of “public information”, why not provide this? If you want people to be able to underwrite $BP’s value, give them the bare minimum information to do that. Most projects do this or most have it available onchain. I would think a team that prides itself on rising from the ashes of being former Alameda, FTX, and Serum team members would see the need for transparency.
-and describing the structure as “progressive”. I’m sorry but I vehemently disagree and see the structure as inferior to the 2026 norm. Many projects now such as Hyperliquid and Lighter have eliminated the equity-token conflict altogether by having all value accrue to the token. Others will completely merge the concept of equity and token. That’s progress. The chance at 20% equity 4+ years down the road seems like 10 steps back from common 2026 structures.

My quick thesis on decision models, since I've been having a lot of conversations about this lately:

LLMs are amazing because they are fully general. You can use them for pretty much anything. But they are slow, expensive, and too unreliable to embed in software at runtime. Unless your product is literally chat, real-time LLM calls are unworkable for the majority of use cases. (Especially in finance!)

Decision models change that. To abuse an analogy, they are the ASICs of LLMs. They give up the generality of an LLM, but in exchange for constraining your outputs, you get MASSIVE gains in cost-efficiency, throughput, and latency.

In the early days of the AI boom, people understandably tried to shove LLMs into everything. But like with ASICs, you will eventually constrain your problem enough to burn it into the machine. Once your problem is an if-else, a buy or sell, a label, a choice, or a well-defined state machine like an onchain smart contract, a decision model will clobber the LLM on cost, speed, and reliability.

Most systems are not language-in, language-out.

Going forward, LLMs will write our code (since coding is high-dimensional and general), but that code will embed decision models to make runtime software intelligent and capable.

That's the bet we're making with Typesafe. They identified this path and proved that it works. 25%+ of the Fortune 500 is already using Jev, and it launched less than a month ago.

Of course, there are murmurings on the timeline that decision models are easy to copy. OpenAI, Microsoft, Amazon, and Cloudflare have all launched decision models in the weeks since Jev launched, realizing that this is going to be an enormous market and they don't want to lose it.

To be sure, anyone can lop off the last layer of Qwen, fine-tune it to create a classifier, and copy the Typesafe SDK's API. But there's a lot more that goes into a world-class decision model, and there's a reason why Jev is still cheaper, faster, and more general than these other alternatives. (Decision model benchmarking started all of 10 minutes ago, but if you ask devs who've tried them, they'll tell you Jev is far and away the best right now.)

There's no guarantee that lead lasts forever though. Decision models are too big of a market to be able to coast into a monopoly. From here, the onus is on them. They have to keep training better models ($$ helps), ship great products, serve their models better, faster, and cheaper than anyone else (many more tricks there), and win developers with their community-first philosophy. But they've been at this for years and have a lot up their sleeves (they were expecting a bevy of copycats if Jev took off). Diogo knows from his years at OpenAI how to sustain a research advantage. And as with all startups, focus is how you beat the incumbents.

Super bullish on this team.

And if you're a dev and you haven't tried Jev yet, get on it.

China’s industrial profit growth is losing momentum:

China’s industrial profits rose +4.2% YoY in August, the weakest YoY growth since November 2025.

This also marks the 4th consecutive monthly slowdown in growth.

Pressure is particularly visible in consumer-facing industries, where profits are falling in autos, clothing, and furniture.

Domestic demand continues to weaken, with consumption growth slowing to near zero while manufacturers, property developers, and infrastructure builders are cutting spending.

For the first 8 months of 2026, industrial profits were still up +15.7% YoY, but the gains are becoming increasingly concentrated, with the electronics industry contributing ~66% of total growth.

At the same time, raw-material industries contributed +6.2 percentage points to the overall increase, supported by higher commodity prices.

Weak domestic demand is weighing on China’s economy.

The US deficit is surging despite low unemployment.

The cumulative US fiscal deficit since 2020 has surged to a massive $14.18 trillion.

In the first 11 months of FY2026 alone, the US deficit totaled $1.97 trillion, the 3rd-largest for this period of the year in history.

This time, however, the deficit is running at historically high levels despite stable unemployment.

This comes as elevated government spending and rising interest costs are keeping the deficit exceptionally large even without a recession.

Massive deficits have become a permanent feature of the US economy.

Shocking stat of the day:

$241 billion worth of French corporate bonds are now trading at lower yields than French government bonds.

This figure is up +1,621% from just $14 billion at the start of 2026.

This means ~38% of French high-grade corporate debt is now trading at lower yields than government bonds of similar maturity.

The gap between corporate and government bond yields is widening as investor concerns about France's deteriorating fiscal situation weigh on government debt.

As a result, internationally exposed companies such as L'Oreal, $OR, and TotalEnergies, $TTE, are increasingly viewed as safer alternatives to French government debt, unlike French banks, which remain more exposed to sovereign risk.

This is in stark contrast to normal economic conditions, when government bonds are traditionally viewed as the safest part of the bond market.

France's corporate bond market is increasingly being treated a safer bet than its government bonds.

3️⃣ Open interest vs volume
Volume tells us how much was traded over a period, while open interest (OI) tells us the value of positions still open at a given moment.

A trader can open and close positions all day, adding to volume each time, but finish with no open position.

So @HyperliquidX’s lead here means it holds the largest share of open positions by value, but it doesn’t mean it has the most traders or that every market is easy to exit.

So @HyperliquidX’s lead here means it holds the largest share of open positions by value, but it doesn’t mean it has the most traders or that every market is easy to exit.

My takeaway: more perp trading is moving onchain, and the range of assets is growing, but I’d still look beyond headline volume to understand what’s driving that activity and whether it lasts.

Good question! Just some informal thoughts... there's three "moats" to look at for $SIVE:

- Capacity 
- Qualifications (especially for custom DFB lasers)
- Technological

1. For capacity, they're coming online with 100M+ CW DFB lasers Q4 2027 (global supply is roughly ~608M EML/CW lasers currently per Trendforce). 

Obviously by 2027 global capacity is going to grow a lot, with $AAOI, $AVGO (3x expansion), and others coming online.  

But if you extrapolate their 2:1 statement, that implies 300m lasers/year long term coming from their own supply + external foundries. 

This is incredibly valuable during a shortage that was quoted to be 3-5 years, and $LITE stating they already have demand visibility into 2031...

And when suppliers have started to qualify many more (eg. 5-7 vendors vs. 2-3 earlier) due to bottlenecks. 

I'm sure a lot of how they achieve that staggering amount is due to their manufacturing process/yields (which is a moat). 

2. For qualifications, if you look at 70mW/100mW pluggable lines with Chinese players, I'd argue this is more generic and moreso reverting back to a capacity  argument and manufacturing process to achieve those numbers. 

Custom DFB arrays that they've been working on with Ayar (they hinted at 2-3 others back in 2023 like Celestial) take years for optical i/o related things and would be a moat if they finish quals. 

So it's not quite something you can hot swap or design out really easily for $MTSI or another company. But of course cpo scale up and such is mass volume in 2028, and we're still H2 2026. 

3. People can always compare raw specs like power output, but it's probably way way more nuanced so easier to just point toward customer statements. 

With $JBL 1.6T LRO: "I think that there's the potential for a relatively dramatic moat with our LRO part…" from Jabil's EVP, especially related to power consumption. And $SIVE is my guess sole source in this line. 

Jabil is probably the most important testament to how their lasers perform in mass production scenarios maybe around Q2 next year. 

Ayar said something similar along the lines of "we couldn't do it without Sivers" for custom implementations.

DeFi has around $91B in TVL right now.

But how much of that money is actually protected if something goes wrong? The money set aside to cover losses is only about 0.14% of that.

We spend hours comparing vault APYs and strategies, but rarely check what happens if a protocol gets exploited. 

It’s like obsessing over a car’s horsepower and skipping the insurance.

DeFi already has protection options. The problem is that most vaults don't include them, leaving users to arrange to cover themselves.

Interestingly, @Firelightfi recently launched a different approach to this, where the vault operator sets up the cover so every depositor gets it automatically.

Here's how it works.

If a covered vault suffers an eligible exploit, five independent security firms review the incident against predefined terms. Once validated, eligible losses can be paid from the capital backing the cover, subject to coverage limits.

The money behind those payouts comes from people staking $FXRP, which is basically $XRP brought over to the Flare network. They earn rewards for taking on that risk, and there’s already 50M+ FXRP staked.

It’s live on Sentora’s USD and RWA vaults, and Veda and Upshift have plugged it in so vaults built on them can switch it on anytime.

I wouldn’t treat this as a guarantee. It only covers specific events like hacks and oracle attacks, and the terms still matter.

But having protection built into a vault, rather than making everyone arrange it separately is kinda how this should’ve worked from the start.

$1.3B in tokens unlocks in October. 

Here are the 5 I'm watching, and the 4 things that tell you whether an unlock actually dumps:

- $PUMP (Oct 11): ~$41.5M unlocking, around 1.5% of supply. Up roughly 12% over the 7 days after its previous unlock on Sep 11.

- $APT (Oct 11): ~$8.5M unlocking, around 0.6% of supply. After its previous unlock on Sep 11, APT fell roughly 7% over the next 7 days.

- $STRK (Oct 15): ~$6.2M unlocking, around 3.4% of supply. 

The ironic part? STRK gained roughly 73% in the 7 days after its Sep 14 unlock.

- $ARB (Oct 16): ~$17M unlocking, around 1.6% of supply. ARB was up roughly 69% in the week after its Sep 15 unlock.

- $ZRO (Oct 20): ~$54M unlocking, around 4% of supply. Its Sep 19 unlock was followed by roughly a 45% gain over the next 7 days.

The obvious mistake here would be looking at those September returns and assuming the same thing happens again.

A lot of that was the market. $BTC went from ~$63k in mid-August to the high $80s by Mid-September, sentiment flipped bullish, and alts caught the wave right as these unlocks were hitting.

The better question is what actually happens to the new tokens.

HYPE is the best example from this week. Its unlock looked huge on paper, but a large part of the team allocation being claimed was sold OTC to a single institutional buyer instead of immediately hitting the open market.

That’s why I’d care more about:

1. how big the unlock is vs supply
2. who receives it
3. whether those tokens move to exchanges
4. what the market is doing at the same time

For most of these, the tokens go to the team, core contributors, and strategic partners, so that part doesn't separate them much. Size does, which is why $ZRO and $STRK get most of my attention at 4% and 3.4% of supply.

Which upcoming unlock are you watching most closely?

tweets.text:
Thank you @PrefShares  for engaging with a constructive and thoughtful response. (anyone curious to read my original piece, go here: https://t.co/U4QGuHSaDw)

Let me take your points in turn.

Retail. I like Amazon’s retail business too, and I agree there are losses buried in ex-AWS. But the profit engine in core retail today is advertising, and I think it’s fair to say ads carries a question mark right now. Consumer agents on one side, the FTC case, the auction-mechanics issues or the bid shading possibilities I’ve written about on the other (see here: https://t.co/JsORiT52qY) 

My base case is still that Amazon figures it out, but it’s not unreasonable to wonder that there is a legitimate fat tail risk to Amazon’s ability to COMPOUND core retail profits which can (should?) weigh on the multiple we may want to put on these profits. Also on $WMT, I haven’t met an $AMZN shareholder yet who thinks WMT is attractive at ~28x LTM EBIT.

Okay, let me now get to AWS.

Cost curve. On the $NVDA discount, I think the argument runs into NVIDIA itself. The hyperscalers are the only customers also building chips to displace it, so NVIDIA has every reason not to hand them a structural cost advantage, and it hasn’t: equity in the neoclouds, capacity backstop, or direct financing for OpenAI to buy gigawatts with no hyperscaler in between…Jensen has made it abundantly clear he doesn’t want to operate in a world where Hyperscalers call the shot. Whatever discount the hyperscalers get, NVIDIA likely hands back to the marginal producer in cheaper capital and risk sharing.

Power is a few percent of a gigawatt-year’s revenue, so cheaper PPAs are worth maybe a point or two, and unlikely to be a needle mover for overall economics. And cost of capital advantage is shared by all Hyperscalers, and also an advantage that is directly being largely negated by NVIDIA with their balance sheet support to neoclouds.

I do agree it’s not obvious to me either why neoclouds have a DURABLE advantage over hyperscalers. But the capacity they’ve bult and are building is pretty real. If AI demand disappoints or we hit a digestion period, the neocloud equities will get obliterated but the gigawatts stay, get repriced, and pressure everyone, hyperscalers included. The concern again is that NVIDIA has an obvious interest in keeping its buyer side VERY fragmented.

Short-term margins. No argument there. Everyone selling compute today is making money hand over fist. The question is whether 2026 is representative of medium and long-term economics. If it is, AWS isn’t $1.3T; it’s comfortably over $2T.

Bedrock as a capital-light royalty. Not sure I agree with your framing, and I think the simplest way is to follow the token. When an enterprise buys a Claude token on Bedrock, it’s generated on a Trainium chip, in an AWS data center, that AWS paid for. That chip is already in my gigawatt count. So whatever AWS keeps on that token I don't see it as a royalty on someone else’s capital, it’s just a markup on its own. Capital-light royalties do exist in AI, but they accrue to whoever owns the weights: Anthropic earns one when $GOOGL sells Claude through Vertex or $MSFT sells it through Foundry (their chips, their utilization risk, Anthropic’s cut). More importantly, let’s notice who will set the royalty rate. The enterprise pays roughly Anthropic’s list price on Bedrock, so AWS’s cut comes out of Anthropic’s margin and Anthropic, which can serve the identical token through its own API, Vertex or Foundry, decides how big that cut is (if not today, they will over time). A royalty where the payer sets both the product price and the royalty rate SHOULD/WILL be a thin one.

Enterprise / other AI. I agree with all six of your points. Those points are why that bucket earns ~2 points over its cost of capital in my model rather than zero. I know 2 points may seem a little low, but the invested capital in that bucket is $468B in 2035, so that’s ~$10B a year of economic profit. I’m hesitant to extrapolate to much more. All six advantages are more or less shared by AWS, Azure and GCP, so they’re a moat against neoclouds and the labs’ direct APIs, but probably not much against each other. The neoclouds know serving hyperscalers and labs isn’t durable, which is precisely why they’re trying to move into this segment as well. And the labs themselves are building first-party products for the same customers. Five to ten points of excess return on a ~$500B base would be $25–50B a year of rent on an input with growing number of alternatives. I’ll admit I am far from certain where that shakes out (could be anywhere between 1 and 5 points IMO).

Core cloud. Fair it’s hard to separate from AI, and AI is clearly helping it. That’s why core grows ~21% in 2026 in my model, well above the ~13% it had slowed to before AI, when optimization was the story. My model still triples the core to ~$360B by 2035. But yes, reasonable people can land above me here.

The key point I was trying to drive home is the exercise actually helped me tone DOWN my own bearish “vibes” on AWS a bit once I realized market is actually fairly skeptical about AWS capex being value additive. The objective of making the assumptions explicit is to see if I perceive any vehement disagreement with what the market is underwriting. Following the exercise, I just realized I do not have such strong disagreement. Market and I are more or less likely on the same boat in evaluating AWS long-term future.

Thanks again. Always a pleasure to have diligent readers.

Having spent 10 years building AI products, this resonates a lot.

Machine learning has long been a black box. Now we’re giving a much more capable black box access to our most sensitive data and the ability to act on our behalf.

Alignment is still a huge challenge. We may never fully understand why a model made a particular decision or which training data shaped it. We need guardrails around it that hold even when the model gets things wrong.

An email agent can have read-only access: it can summarize your inbox, but it has no permission to send anything. Through Entra ID, an agent acting on your behalf stays within explicitly granted permissions and your existing access.

These boundaries need to be enforced outside the model. Same for action logs, spending limits and the ability to stop it mid-task.

“Don’t do this” in a prompt is a request. Removing the permission is a control.

This is everything I admired about America as a teenager growing up in France.

Michael Dell starts a company at 19 in his dorm room with $1,000, becomes a billionaire, then he and Susan commit $6.25 billion to give 25 million American children their first investment.

I remember my high school teachers blaming large corporations and their dividends. It was just accepted in the classroom: corporations were evil, dividends were evil.

And I remember thinking: wait. There’s a system where I can buy a piece of these companies, and they’ll give me money on a recurring basis?

Everyone was explaining why this was terrible, and all I could think was: I need a piece of that. If I want to escape poverty, I need to own some of these businesses.

It took me years to understand investing properly. I hope these kids get that realization much sooner.

Munger said: “Show me the incentive and I’ll show you the outcome.”

You can explain the benefits of capitalism forever. But owning a piece of a business gives you a personal reason to understand profits, dividends, reinvestment and compounding.

Suddenly, America’s most successful companies are partly yours. Their success means something to you.

And maybe a kid who starts by asking “What do I own?” will eventually ask “What could I build?”

That’s what makes this so inspiring to me. A man who built his fortune giving millions of children a first experience of ownership, and perhaps the ambition to build something themselves.

This is the America I dreamed of.
